items.text: You are shown an ultrasound image of a woman in early pregnancy. Interpret the findings.
A pregnant woman presents with vaginal bleeding. Interpret her ultrasound scan.
You are shown a 12-week scan. Identify the structures and explain the findings.
Interpret a 20-week fetal anomaly scan.
A woman at 32 weeks has an ultrasound showing reduced fetal growth. Explain the findings and management.
Interpret an ultrasound report showing placenta praevia.
A scan suggests multiple pregnancy. Describe the type of twin pregnancy.
Counsel a pregnant woman following an ultrasound diagnosis of fetal abnormality.

blocks.text: Your objective: describe the findings, interpret their significance, identify any urgent concerns, and propose appropriate next steps.

blocks.title: If the station involves reviewing a scan with a patient, begin with:

items.text: Wash your hands and introduce yourself.
Confirm the patient's identity.
Explain the purpose of the scan or the results discussion.
Obtain consent before performing an ultrasound examination.
Ask about the last menstrual period, cycle regularity and current gestational age.
Establish the indication for the scan and any relevant symptoms, particularly pain, vaginal bleeding or reduced fetal movements.
Maintain privacy, dignity and confidentiality.
Explain findings in plain language, avoid premature conclusions and allow the patient to ask questions.

blocks.text: If the station is purely image interpretation, you do not need to simulate a physical ultrasound examination. Instead, state that you would confirm the patient's details, gestational age, scan indication and relevant clinical history before interpreting the image.
1. Transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS)

items.text: Particularly useful in early pregnancy.
Provides detailed views of the uterus, gestational sac, yolk sac, embryo and adnexa.
Helps assess pregnancy location and viability.
Requires informed consent, privacy and appropriate preparation.

blocks.text: 2. Transabdominal ultrasound

items.text: Commonly used throughout pregnancy.
Assesses fetal growth, anatomy, lie, presentation, placenta and amniotic fluid.
An adequately filled bladder may improve views during some early-pregnancy scans.
A full bladder is generally unnecessary later in pregnancy.

blocks.text: 3. Doppler ultrasound

items.text: Assesses blood flow in selected maternal and fetal vessels.
Umbilical artery Doppler is important in suspected fetal growth restriction.
Middle cerebral artery Doppler may be used in selected situations, including fetal anaemia assessment.
Uterine artery Doppler may contribute to pre-eclampsia or placental dysfunction risk assessment.

content_groups.group_title: B. Identify the indication before interpreting the image

blocks.text: Ask yourself: Why was this scan requested?

items.text: Early pregnancy: confirm pregnancy location, viability, gestational age and number of embryos.
First trimester screening: assess dating and, where appropriate, markers used in aneuploidy screening.
Mid-trimester: assess fetal anatomy and screen for structural abnormalities.
Third trimester: assess growth, presentation, placental location and amniotic fluid when indicated.
Suspected complications: investigate bleeding, pain, multiple pregnancy, fetal growth restriction, abnormal liquor volume or placental problems.

blocks.text: Remember: not every pregnant woman needs every type of ultrasound. The scan schedule depends on local policy, clinical indication and available services.

subsections.subsection_title: 4. Step-by-step method for interpreting any obstetric ultrasound

blocks.text: Use the mnemonic P–V–G–F–P–L–A–D.
Pregnancy location
Is the pregnancy intrauterine? Are there features suggesting an ectopic pregnancy?
Viability
Is cardiac activity seen when expected? Are the findings definitive or indeterminate?
Gestational age
Assess CRL in early pregnancy or appropriate fetal biometric measurements later.
Fetal number and anatomy
Count fetuses and assess anatomy appropriate to the stage of pregnancy.
Placenta
Describe location, relationship to the internal cervical os and any suspicious abnormalities.
Liquor
Assess amniotic fluid volume using the appropriate method.
Assessment of growth
Review estimated fetal weight, abdominal circumference and growth trajectory.
Doppler and other details
Review Doppler findings when indicated, fetal presentation, cervix and adnexa as relevant.
You should adapt this sequence to the scan's gestational age and clinical indication. Not every element is assessable or required on every scan.

rows: Its location, appearance and mean sac diameter where appropriate
Supports identification of an early intrauterine pregnancy
Supports viability at the time of examination
May reveal an ectopic pregnancy or adnexal mass
May be clinically significant, particularly with pain or bleeding

blocks.text: An intrauterine fluid collection alone is not always definitive evidence of an intrauterine pregnancy. Look for appropriate gestational structures and interpret the findings in context.
Crown–rump length (CRL) is the preferred ultrasound measurement for dating a pregnancy in the first trimester when the embryo can be measured reliably.

items.text: CRL is measured from the top of the embryo's head to its rump.
The measurement is used with a validated dating chart or ultrasound system.
The earliest reliable ultrasound measurement is generally the best basis for establishing gestational age.
Do not estimate gestational age from the gestational sac alone when a more reliable embryo measurement is available.

blocks.text: Example: A scan performed at approximately 9 weeks shows an embryo with a CRL corresponding to 9 weeks and visible cardiac activity. If the clinical history is consistent, the pregnancy can be dated using that CRL measurement.

content_groups.group_title: C. Assessing viability: a critical OSCE safety point

blocks.text: Do not diagnose miscarriage from a single uncertain finding.

blocks.title: Commonly used conservative transvaginal ultrasound criteria include:

items.text: CRL of 7 mm or more with no visible cardiac activity: diagnostic criterion for pregnancy failure under widely used consensus criteria, after appropriate technical assessment.
Mean gestational sac diameter of 25 mm or more with no embryo: diagnostic criterion under widely used consensus criteria.

blocks.text: If measurements fall below these thresholds or the scan is technically uncertain, the findings may be indeterminate. Arrange repeat ultrasound at an appropriate interval, commonly at least 7 days depending on the findings and applicable guideline, and seek experienced review.
Clinical management must also account for symptoms, scan quality and the possibility of ectopic pregnancy. Do not delay urgent assessment in an unstable patient.
Ectopic pregnancy
Findings may include an adnexal mass separate from the ovary, an extrauterine gestational sac or an extrauterine embryo. Free fluid may indicate haemoperitoneum.
Action: assess haemodynamic stability immediately. Suspected rupture requires emergency gynaecological management.
Early pregnancy loss
May show an embryo without cardiac activity meeting accepted diagnostic criteria, or a gestational sac without an embryo meeting accepted criteria.
Action: confirm diagnostic criteria and counsel sensitively. Offer appropriate expectant, medical or surgical management according to clinical circumstances and patient preference.
Molar pregnancy
Ultrasound may show heterogeneous echogenic intrauterine tissue with multiple cystic spaces. The classic appearance may be absent in early disease.
Action: refer for specialist assessment, quantitative hCG evaluation and appropriate management and follow-up.
Other possibilities include a pregnancy of unknown location, subchorionic haematoma and an adnexal mass unrelated to pregnancy.

Pregnancy of unknown location (PUL) means a pregnancy test is positive but transvaginal ultrasound has not identified a definite intrauterine or ectopic pregnancy. It is a temporary classification requiring follow-up, not a final diagnosis. Serial hCG measurements and repeat ultrasound may be required.
The routine mid-trimester anomaly scan is commonly performed at approximately 18–22 weeks, although the exact window depends on the local screening programme.
Use the mnemonic H–B–F–S–A–P–L.

items.text: H — Head and brain: skull, cerebral structures and ventricles.
B — Body and abdomen: abdominal wall, stomach, kidneys and bladder as appropriate.
F — Face: facial profile and other required facial views.
S — Spine: alignment and appearance of the vertebral column.
A — Anatomy of the heart: four-chamber view and additional cardiac views required by the protocol.
P — Placenta: location and relationship to the cervix.
L — Limbs: presence, alignment and appearance of the limbs.

blocks.text: Also assess fetal number, biometry, amniotic fluid and cervix when indicated by the protocol.
A screening scan cannot exclude every congenital abnormality. Some abnormalities develop later, are difficult to visualise or cannot be detected prenatally.

content_groups.group_title: B. Common abnormalities shown in OSCE images

blocks.text: 1. Open spina bifida
Possible findings include a spinal defect, abnormal posterior fossa and associated cranial signs such as the lemon and banana signs.
Next steps: detailed fetal medicine assessment, counselling and evaluation for associated abnormalities.
2. Anencephaly
There is major absence of the cranial vault and cerebral structures.
Next steps: prompt specialist confirmation, compassionate counselling and discussion of options and care in accordance with applicable law and local policy.
3. Ventriculomegaly
The lateral ventricles are enlarged. An atrial width of 10 mm or more is generally considered ventriculomegaly.
Next steps: detailed neurosonography, assessment for associated abnormalities and specialist-directed investigations.
4. Omphalocele
Abdominal contents protrude through the umbilical region and are covered by a membrane.
Next steps: detailed anatomical assessment, consideration of associated chromosomal or structural abnormalities, and multidisciplinary planning.

Other important conditions include gastroschisis, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, congenital heart defects, renal abnormalities, limb defects and markers that may alter the risk of chromosomal conditions.

content_groups.group_title: C. What if an abnormality is suspected?

blocks.text: In the OSCE, do not announce a definitive diagnosis beyond what the image supports.
A good response is:

“The ultrasound appears to show a possible structural fetal abnormality. I would arrange prompt review by a fetal medicine specialist for confirmation, assess for associated abnormalities, and provide sensitive, non-directive counselling to the parents.”

subsections.subsection_title: 7. Third-trimester ultrasound: growth and fetal wellbeing

items.text: The BPD can be measured through any plane that crosses the 3rd ventricle, thalami, and cavum septi pellucidi (CSP).
The calvaria should be smooth and symmetrical as indicated.
The cursor in the near field should be placed on the outer edge of the calvaria and the cursor in the far field should be placed on the inner edge as indicated.

blocks.text: Above. For the HC measurement:

1. Measurement is through a plane that crosses the 3rd ventricle, thalami, and CSP.
2. The calvaria should be smooth and symmetrical.
3. The cavum septi pellucidi (CSP) should be visible in the anterior portion of the brain.
4. Caliper placement is around the calvarial wall and should not include scalp thickness.
The CSP appears as a box like structure in the anterior portion of the brain as demonstrated. The hyperechoic lines represent the medial walls of the lateral ventricle.

The 3-lined structure is not the CSP and represents the columns of the fornix. The fornix represents paired nerve columns, which are located just inferior to the CSP. The transaxial view when the fornix is seen suggests that the transducer plane is just inferior to the proper plane to obtain the CSP.
Note the difference between the box like structure, the CSP, and the structure with 3 parallel lines, which represent the columns of the fornix.

The CI is an index or ratio which is used to evaluate the shape of the head. It is calculated by measuring the maximum width (BPD) of the cranium divided by its maximum length (occipital frontal diameter, OFD). The front to back, OFD, is measured with the cursor placed on the outer edge to outer edge of the cranial bones as demonstrated. The following formula derives the cephalic index:
CI =BPD/OFD x 100
A normal cephalic index (CI) = 78.3%
1 Standard Deviation (SD) = 74%-83%
2 Standard Deviations (SD) = 70%-86%

Dolicocephaly is defined when the AP diameter is longer than the transverse diameter and the CI is <70% (> 2 SD). Dolicocephaly may be seen in a number of conditions, including oligohydrmnios and multiple gestations.

Brachycephaly is defined when the transverse diameter is greater than the AP (anterior posterior) diameter and the CI is > 86% (> 2 SD). Brachycephaly may be seen in a number of conditions including synostosis, trisomy 21, and hydrocephalus.

The AC measurement should be taken at the skin line on a true transverse view at the level of the junction of the umbilical vein, portal sinus, and fetal stomach. At this location, the liver size is reflected. The visualized ribs should be symmetrical. The abdomen should not be compressed during image acquisition.
Correct AC measurement. Note placement of cursor outside skin line. Again, ribs are symmetrical. The stomach is seen and both the umbilical vein and portal sinus are identified.
Incorrect imaging of AC. Note that the portal sinus is not seen, the rib images are not symmetrical, and the stomach is not well visualized.
The liver is visualized, but the portal sinus is not well defined. The rib images are not symmetrical and the stomach is not well visualized.

The liver is visualized, but the umbilical vein is not seen and the portal sinus is not well defined. The kidney should not be in the field of view. The stomach is seen but not in relationship to the umbilical vein or portal sinus.

The long axis of the diaphysis of the femur is most accurately measured when the ultrasound beam of insonation is perpendicular to the shaft. The cartilage at the ends of the femur should not be included in the measurement.
Only the diaphysis should be measured between the epiphysis, which represents the portion of the long bone formed by the primary ossification center.
Note the femoral head which is distinct from the femoral epiphysis.

The principles of HL measurement correspond to those of the femur. The insonation of the ultrasound beam is best directed in a perpendicular fashion and the diaphysis alone is measured after the forearm and shoulder region are identified.
The fetal foot measurement is taken from the tip of the longest toe (typically the second toe) to the tip of the heal.

The ulna is longer than the radius. Note that it extends into the elbow, higher than the radius. The radius is on the thumb side and the ulna is on the 5th digit or little finger side of the forearm. Again, the measurement is easier to establish when the ultrasound beam is perpendicular to the long bone.
Among the bones of the lower leg, the fibula is smaller than the tibia. The tibia is longer than the fibula and the tibia originates closer to the knee compared to the fibula.
The orbits and the lens of the eye can be viewed when both orbits are in a coronal or axial view and are most easily visualized when the fetal head is in a direct occiput posterior position.

The BOD is measured from the outer edge of one orbit to the outer edge of the other orbit. These measurements may be useful in assessing certain syndromes, potential karyotype abnormalities, severe growth restriction, or in assessing fetal age when other measurements are difficult to obtain.
The IOD represents the outer edge to outer edge distance between the orbits. It may be measured for the same reasons that BOD is measured and when facial anomalies are suspected.

rows: Assesses head size and contributes to dating and growth assessment
Measures the length of the femur
Estimates fetal weight from a combination of measurements

blocks.text: EFW is calculated using a validated formula, often involving HC, AC, FL and sometimes BPD. It is an estimate, not the actual fetal weight.

items.text: Small for gestational age (SGA): commonly defined as EFW or AC below the 10th centile.
Fetal growth restriction (FGR): a fetus that has not achieved its growth potential, often because of placental dysfunction or other pathology.
Large for gestational age (LGA): commonly EFW above the 90th centile.
Macrosomia: a high absolute birthweight or estimated fetal weight, defined using a threshold appropriate to the guideline or clinical context.

blocks.text: A fetus below the 10th centile is not automatically growth-restricted, and a fetus above the 10th centile is not guaranteed to be healthy. Interpret measurements alongside growth trajectory, maternal risk factors, liquor volume and Doppler findings.

blocks.title: If an ultrasound shows EFW or AC below the 10th centile:

items.text: Confirm gestational age and review previous growth measurements.
Assess maternal history and risk factors, including hypertension and placental disease.
Arrange appropriate fetal growth surveillance.
Assess amniotic fluid and umbilical artery Doppler.
Consider additional fetal surveillance and investigations according to the severity and gestational age.
Plan delivery timing with the obstetric team, guided by gestational age, Doppler results, maternal condition and fetal wellbeing.

blocks.text: High-yield finding: absent or reversed end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery is concerning for significant placental dysfunction and requires urgent specialist assessment and management.
Oligohydramnios
Commonly defined as a deepest vertical pocket below 2 cm. An amniotic fluid index (AFI) of 5 cm or less is another commonly used threshold.
Consider membrane rupture, placental insufficiency, fetal renal or urinary tract abnormalities and relevant medications.
Polyhydramnios
Commonly defined as a deepest vertical pocket of 8 cm or more or AFI of 24–25 cm or more, depending on the guideline.
Consider maternal diabetes, fetal swallowing or gastrointestinal abnormalities, fetal anaemia and other causes.
Do not diagnose abnormal liquor volume by visual impression alone when a validated measurement is available.

items.text: Anterior placenta: attached to the anterior uterine wall.
Posterior placenta: attached to the posterior uterine wall.
Fundal placenta: located near the uterine fundus.
Low-lying placenta: placental edge less than 20 mm from the internal cervical os after 16 weeks, according to commonly used definitions.
Placenta praevia: placenta covers the internal cervical os.

blocks.text: A low-lying placenta detected at the mid-trimester scan may no longer be low-lying later in pregnancy as the lower uterine segment develops. Follow-up imaging is important when indicated.

If placenta praevia is suspected, transvaginal ultrasound is generally safe when performed appropriately and is more accurate for measuring the placental edge-to-os distance. Avoid an unplanned digital vaginal examination in a patient with suspected placenta praevia and bleeding until the clinical team has appropriately assessed the situation.
The key question in a twin pregnancy is not just how many fetuses are present, but whether they share a placenta and/or amniotic sac.

rows: Two chorions and two amniotic sacs
May be two placentas or fused placentas

blocks.text: The lambda or twin-peak sign may support dichorionicity; the T-sign may support monochorionic diamniotic pregnancy. These signs must be interpreted with the complete scan, especially in early pregnancy.
OSCE tip: chorionicity is best established in the first trimester because the relevant features may become less clear as pregnancy advances.
Monochorionic pregnancies need specialist surveillance because of complications such as twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome and selective fetal growth restriction.

subsections.subsection_title: 9. Common O&G ultrasound findings: differential diagnosis and management

rows: Positive pregnancy test, no pregnancy seen
Assess symptoms, serial hCG and repeat TVUS as indicated
Adnexal gestational sac or suspicious mass
Urgent clinical assessment; emergency management if unstable
Very early pregnancy or pregnancy failure
Apply conservative diagnostic criteria; repeat scan if uncertain
Heterogeneous tissue with multiple cystic spaces
Specialist review, hCG assessment and follow-up
Review growth trajectory, liquor and Doppler
Assess severity and investigate possible causes
Assess membrane status, fetal growth and wellbeing
Detailed fetal assessment and specialist referral
Confirm findings and arrange fetal medicine review

blocks.text: These are starting points rather than definitive diagnoses. The clinical history, gestational age and complete ultrasound examination determine the appropriate interpretation.

subsections.subsection_title: 10. Investigations following an abnormal obstetric ultrasound

blocks.text: Investigations depend on the finding; they should not all be ordered routinely.
Early pregnancy bleeding or pregnancy of unknown location

items.text: Quantitative serum β-hCG, often repeated approximately 48 hours later when clinically appropriate.
Repeat transvaginal ultrasound.
Full blood count and blood group/Rh status as indicated by bleeding severity and local protocol.
Urgent assessment if ectopic pregnancy or significant haemorrhage is suspected.

blocks.text: Suspected fetal growth restriction

items.text: Serial growth ultrasound.
Umbilical artery Doppler.
Amniotic fluid assessment.
Maternal blood pressure and evaluation for pre-eclampsia when indicated.
CTG or other fetal surveillance according to gestational age and clinical risk.

blocks.text: Suspected fetal structural abnormality

items.text: Detailed fetal anomaly scan or targeted ultrasound.
Fetal echocardiography when indicated.
Genetic counselling and diagnostic testing, such as amniocentesis, when appropriate.
Additional investigations directed by the suspected abnormality.

blocks.text: Suspected placenta accreta spectrum

items.text: Detailed ultrasound by an experienced operator, including Doppler where indicated.
MRI in selected cases when it may clarify the diagnosis or extent.
Specialist multidisciplinary planning for delivery.

subsections.subsection_title: 11. How to report an obstetric ultrasound in the OSCE

blocks.text: The examiner wants a systematic report, not merely the name of a diagnosis.

items.text: Patient and indication: relevant clinical history and gestational age.
Technique: transabdominal, transvaginal or both.
Pregnancy: intrauterine or extrauterine; singleton or multiple.
Viability: cardiac activity, where appropriate.
Dating and biometry: CRL or appropriate fetal measurements.
Anatomy: normal structures visualised and any abnormalities.
Placenta: location and relationship to the internal cervical os.
Liquor: normal, reduced or increased, with measurements where available.
Growth and Doppler: EFW centile, growth trend and relevant Doppler results.
Impression and plan: summary, limitations and recommended next steps.

blocks.text: “The scan demonstrates a single intrauterine pregnancy with an embryo measuring approximately 9 weeks by crown–rump length. Cardiac activity is present. The gestational age is consistent with the biometric measurement. No obvious abnormality is identified in the structures assessed. I would correlate the findings with the clinical history and issue the formal report.”

“The scan demonstrates no definite intrauterine pregnancy and an abnormal adnexal finding suspicious for an ectopic pregnancy. I would assess the patient’s haemodynamic status immediately, review the adnexa and pelvic free fluid, and arrange urgent gynaecological assessment. If the patient is unstable or rupture is suspected, emergency management is required.”
Do not report ectopic pregnancy as confirmed unless the imaging findings support that conclusion.

“The scan demonstrates a placenta covering the internal cervical os, consistent with placenta praevia. I would confirm the placental relationship to the os, assess for relevant risk factors and features of placenta accreta spectrum, and arrange specialist obstetric follow-up and delivery planning.”

“The fetus has an estimated fetal weight below the 10th centile for the established gestational age, raising concern for a small-for-gestational-age fetus or fetal growth restriction. I would review serial growth measurements, amniotic fluid volume and umbilical artery Doppler, assess maternal risk factors and plan further surveillance with the obstetric team.”

“The amniotic fluid volume is reduced, with a deepest vertical pocket below 2 cm. I would assess for rupture of membranes, review fetal growth and renal anatomy where relevant, evaluate fetal wellbeing and arrange management according to the gestational age and clinical findings.”
Q1. What is the best ultrasound parameter for dating a first-trimester pregnancy?
Answer: Crown–rump length, measured in a technically adequate scan and interpreted using a validated dating chart.
Q2. What are the criteria for diagnosing early pregnancy failure on transvaginal ultrasound?

Answer: Widely used conservative criteria include CRL of at least 7 mm without cardiac activity, or mean gestational sac diameter of at least 25 mm without an embryo. The scan must be technically adequate and interpreted appropriately. Findings below these thresholds generally require follow-up rather than an immediate diagnosis.
Q3. What is a pregnancy of unknown location?

Answer: A positive pregnancy test with no definite intrauterine or ectopic pregnancy identified on transvaginal ultrasound. Follow-up is required until the pregnancy location or outcome is established.
Q4. What is the difference between SGA and FGR?

Answer: SGA describes a fetus smaller than expected for gestational age, commonly below the 10th centile. FGR implies pathological failure to achieve growth potential. Doppler abnormalities, growth trajectory and clinical risk factors help distinguish them.
Q5. What are the common ultrasound definitions of oligohydramnios and polyhydramnios?

Answer: Oligohydramnios is commonly defined as a deepest vertical pocket below 2 cm or AFI of 5 cm or less. Polyhydramnios is commonly defined as a deepest vertical pocket of at least 8 cm or AFI of approximately 24–25 cm or more, depending on the guideline.
Q6. What is the significance of absent end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery?

Answer: It suggests significant placental vascular resistance and increases concern for fetal compromise. Urgent specialist assessment and gestation-specific fetal surveillance and delivery planning are required.
Q7. Is transvaginal ultrasound safe when placenta praevia is suspected?

Answer: Yes. When performed appropriately, it is safe and more accurate than transabdominal ultrasound for assessing the placental edge relative to the internal cervical os. It must not be confused with an unplanned digital vaginal examination.
Q8. What is the difference between a screening scan and a diagnostic test?

Answer: A screening scan identifies pregnancies at increased risk of a condition or detects possible abnormalities. A diagnostic assessment aims to establish whether a specific condition is present. An ultrasound finding may require further imaging or genetic testing for confirmation.
Q9. What are the risks associated with monochorionic twins?
Answer: Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome, selective fetal growth restriction, twin anaemia–polycythaemia sequence and, in monochorionic monoamniotic pregnancies, cord entanglement.
Q10. What should you do if a scan suggests a major fetal anomaly?

Answer: Explain the concern sensitively, arrange specialist confirmation and detailed assessment, offer appropriate genetic counselling and further investigations, and discuss the implications and available options in a non-directive manner.

items.text: Calling a pregnancy non-viable from an early scan that does not meet diagnostic criteria.
Assuming that an empty uterus means ectopic pregnancy without appropriate assessment.
Forgetting that pregnancy of unknown location requires follow-up.
Giving a definitive diagnosis from a single image of poor quality.
Confusing SGA with pathological fetal growth restriction.
Reporting a low-lying placenta as placenta praevia without confirming its relationship to the internal os.
Failing to mention Doppler assessment in suspected FGR.
Reassuring a patient that the anomaly scan excludes all congenital abnormalities.
Discussing a serious fetal abnormality insensitively or before appropriate confirmation.
Ignoring maternal instability in a patient with pain and suspected ectopic pregnancy.

blocks.text: Identify the scan type and clinical indication
Assess pregnancy location and viability when relevant
Interpret gestational age and fetal biometry
Assess fetal number and anatomy
Describe placental location and the internal cervical os
Assess amniotic fluid volume
Review fetal growth and Doppler when indicated
Identify abnormalities and their clinical significance
State appropriate further investigations
Propose management and urgent escalation when required
Deliver a clear, sensitive report to the patient or examiner

items.text: First trimester: location, viability and accurate dating.
Second trimester: fetal anatomy and placental location.
Third trimester: growth, presentation, liquor and Doppler when indicated.
Never diagnose early pregnancy failure from uncertain findings.
Always escalate suspected ectopic rupture, significant fetal compromise or major maternal bleeding.
A good OSCE answer combines description → interpretation → differential diagnosis → investigations → management.
